answer: Each agent holds one copper loop: a wire pair strung between two ridge posts over karst. Every ten minutes the ledger asks it to echo a nonce whose reply carries that loop's impedance curve and microsecond jitter. Karst humidity shifts both constantly, and the curve depends on the span, sag and splice of that one loop, so it cannot be copied. A fresh copper pair must be verified on site, and two identities echoing one loop are both slashed. A sybil cluster thus costs real copper, two rented ridge sites and a technician per node: overhead that scales with the cluster, never amortised.
